scenes.title: Arithmetic Average Returns vs. True Geometric Compounding

beatOutlines.textOutline: Compare Arithmetic Average: (+100% - 50%) / 2 = +25% per year, which severely distorts true portfolio performance ([fact-04], [fact-05]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Compare Geometric Compound Return: $100 growing to $200 and back to $100 results in 0.0% net geometric return and continuously compounded return ([fact-04], [fact-05]).

beatOutlines.textOutline: Break down Log Price Ratio Distribution: ln(S_T/S_0) ~ N((mu - sigma^2/2)*T, sigma^2 * T) and E[S_T] = S_0 * exp(mu * T) ([fact-02], [fact-03]).

beatOutlines.textOutline: Break down Annualized Volatility: s = sqrt((1/(n-1))*sum((u_i - u_bar)^2)) and sigma = s / sqrt(tau) ([fact-06]).

summarySteps: 1. Lognormal Distribution ([fact-01]): Continuously compounded returns ln(S_T / S_0) are normally distributed, ensuring stock prices S_T are lognormal and never drop below zero.
2. Ito's Lemma Convexity Drag ([fact-02]): The drift of log prices is adjusted by subtracting sigma^2 / 2 due to convexity between arithmetic and geometric growth.
3. Arithmetic vs. Geometric Returns ([fact-04], [fact-05]): Arithmetic averages upwardly bias performance by sigma^2 / 2, whereas geometric compounding reflects true wealth changes.
4. Volatility Estimation ([fact-06]): Annualized volatility sigma is calculated from sample standard deviation s of daily log returns divided by square root of observation interval tau.
5. 252 Trading Days Convention ([fact-07], [fact-08]): Kenneth French's 1980 study proved trading activity rather than calendar time drives volatility, validating the 252-day annualization factor.
6. Gross Payoff vs. Net Profit ([fact-09]): Net trading profit equals terminal gross payoff minus initial premium paid (c0).
7. BSM Market Assumptions ([fact-10]): The Black-Scholes-Merton model assumes geometric Brownian motion, continuous trading, short selling, zero transaction costs, and constant r.
8. Cumulative Normal Distribution N(x) ([fact-11]): N(d2) represents exercise probability and N(d1) represents the delta hedge ratio adjusted for stock price growth.
bottomTakeaway: Geometric Brownian motion and lognormal stock pricing form the foundation of the Black-Scholes-Merton model, where annualized volatility and risk-neutral pricing govern option valuation ([fact-01], [fact-02], [fact-06], [fact-08], [fact-10]).
